content: The transfusion of blood and blood products is a critical medical intervention that can save lives. However, it is not without risks. Adverse events can occur both during the donation of blood and its components, as well as during the transfusion process to patients. These adverse events encompass a wide range of issues, including reactions, incidents, near misses, errors, deviations from standard operating procedures, and accidents. Learning from these adverse events and identifying systemic problems is essential. This process enables the implementation of measures to improve the quality, safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of blood and blood products, as well as the donation and transfusion processes. Haemovigilance is a comprehensive surveillance system that monitors the entire transfusion chain, from blood donation and processing to its provision, transfusion to patients, and subsequent follow-up. Haemovigilance involves the systematic monitoring, reporting, investigation, and analysis of adverse events related to blood donation, processing, and transfusion. It also includes the development and implementation of recommendations to prevent the occurrence or recurrence of such events. The ultimate goal of haemovigilance is to achieve continuous quality improvement in the transfusion chain by implementing corrective and preventive actions. This ensures enhanced patient safety, improved outcomes, better donor safety, and reduced wastage of blood products. Haemovigilance systems should be fully integrated into the quality systems of all institutions involved in the donation, processing, storage, distribution, and clinical transfusion of blood and blood products. The organization of a haemovigilance system depends on the structure of the national blood and health systems. A robust haemovigilance system relies on the traceability of blood and blood products from donors to recipients and vice versa, as well as the effective monitoring, reporting, investigation, and analysis of adverse events. The management of information generated through haemovigilance is critical. This data informs amendments to blood policies and guidelines, leading to changes in processes and practices in blood donation and transfusion. Establishing a haemovigilance system requires coordination and collaboration among all stakeholders, including the Ministry of Health, blood transfusion services, hospitals, professional bodies, public health institutions, regulatory agencies, and patient and donor groups. The Ministry of Health (MoH) holds ultimate responsibility for the national blood system, ensuring the quality, safety, and sufficiency of the blood supply. A haemovigilance system contributes to the safety of blood donation, blood products, and transfusion. It enhances risk management, builds trust, and should operate in a confidential and non-punitive manner. The MoH must provide effective leadership and governance for a national haemovigilance system, including comprehensive surveillance of the entire transfusion chain as part of the national blood policy and plan. Key elements of a haemovigilance system include the establishment of standards and definitions aligned with international recommendations, the traceability of blood products from donor to patient, and the implementation of corrective and preventive actions. The system should also define the scope of reporting, including whether it is mandatory, voluntary, or mixed, and the types of events to be reported, such as adverse reactions, near misses, and errors. An efficient haemovigilance system requires clear structures and channels for reporting, investigating, and analyzing adverse events, as well as mechanisms for feedback and communication of findings. It also necessitates guidelines, procedures, and formats for data collection, validation, and analysis. A quality system must be implemented throughout the transfusion chain to address weaknesses and deficiencies promptly. In the context of clinical transfusion, hospitals and healthcare facilities play a critical role. They are responsible for recognizing and managing adverse events associated with transfusion, ensuring the correct identification of patients, samples, and blood products, and implementing hospital standards and clinical guidelines for safe transfusion practices. They must also maintain traceability and documentation of transfused blood products in patient records, respond to product recalls, and actively participate in hospital transfusion committees. Training and assessment of healthcare staff involved in all steps of clinical transfusion are essential. This includes clinical decision-making, pre-transfusion sampling, laboratory practices, handling of blood units, bedside administration, and patient monitoring. Regular audits of clinical transfusion practices and mechanisms for coordination between hospital departments and blood transfusion services are also necessary. In summary, a haemovigilance system is a vital component of the national blood system. It ensures the safety and quality of blood donation and transfusion processes, improves patient and donor outcomes, and fosters trust in the healthcare system. Effective leadership, collaboration among stakeholders, and adherence to international standards are essential for the successful implementation and sustainability of such a system.
